w:r.w:t: An Investigation into the Development of a Smart Restaurant Management Application Integrating Weather-Based Menu Recommendations and Machine Learning-Driven Peak Hours Analytics
The restaurant industry has gone through a significant shift over the last decade. Customers no longer just walk in and pick something from a menu

ed and connected experience. Mobile apps, online reservations, and digital menus have become fairly common. However, even with all this progress, most restaurant applications still work in a pretty generic way. They show a menu, let you book a table, and maybe collect some reviews. What they do not do is adapt to what is happening around the customer in real time, or help restaurant owners make smarter decisions based on actual data patterns.

This gap is what the proposed project aims to address. The idea came from a simple observation food preferences change depending on the weather. On a cold evening, people are more likely to go for something warm and hearty. On a hot afternoon, a cold drink or a light salad makes more sense. Despite this being fairly obvious, no widely used restaurant app currently uses real-time weather data to guide what a customer might want to order. Research in consumer behaviour supports this too. Studies have shown that environmental conditions, including temperature and weather, directly influence food and drink choices (Wansink and Sangerman, 2000). Yet the technology to act on this insight has not been applied in the restaurant app space in any meaningful way.

On the operational side, restaurant managers often struggle with planning. Staffing too many people on a quiet evening wastes money. Being understaffed during a Friday dinner rush leads to poor service and unhappy customers. Traditionally, managers rely on experience and gut feeling to handle this. There is rarely any data-driven system in place that actually analyses historical order patterns and predicts when the restaurant is likely to be busy. Machine learning offers a practical solution to this. Algorithms like Random Forest, which fall under supervised

learning, are well suited for identifying patterns in time-series data such as order timestamps (Breiman, 2001). Using historical order data stored in the database, a trained model can reasonably forecast busy periods and give admins an advance view of what to expect.

It is also worth noting that most restaurant apps treat the customer side and the management side as two separate concerns. There is rarely a single platform that handles both well — one that gives customers a smooth and intelligent ordering and booking experience while also giving the admin a proper dashboard with meaningful data. This project is trying to bring both together under one system.

From a technical standpoint, the tools and technologies involved — React.js, React Native, Node.js, MongoDB, Python, and Scikit-learn are all industry-relevant and widely used. Building this project provides practical exposure to full-stack development, mobile development, API integration, and applied machine learning, all of which are increasingly important in the computing job market. The combination of a real-world problem, a clear technical solution, and the use of current technologies makes this a worthwhile and achievable dissertation project.

To design, develop, and evaluate a full-stack restaurant management application that integrates real-time weather-based menu recommendations and a machine learning-powered peak hours analytics module, with the purpose of improving the dining experience for customers and supporting data-driven operational decision-making for restaurant administrators.
The following objectives have been identified to address the project aim. Each objective is specific, measurable, and aligned to a stage of the dissertation:
Identify key research context and existing literature

Review existing restaurant management applications, examine research on weather-based consumer behaviour and food choice, and investigate how machine learning has been applied to demand forecasting in the hospitality sector. This will form the basis of the literature review.
Gather and document user and system requirements
Define the functional and non-functional requirements of the system through user research methods such as a questionnaire distributed to potential users and a structured
interview with at least one restaurant operator. Requirements to be documented and signed off by Week 6.

Design and build the core restaurant management features: a dual-panel system for users and admins, online table reservation, dynamic menu management, and a customer feedback module. All core features to be functional and testable by Week 12.
Implement the weather-based menu recommendation feature

Integrate a live weather API (such as OpenWeatherMap) into the application so that menu suggestions presented to users are dynamically filtered based on the current weather conditions at the restaurant location. This feature to be integrated and tested by Week 14.
Develop and integrate the machine learning peak hours prediction module

using Scikit-learn (Random Forest algorithm) that analyses historical order data from MongoDB, identifies peak hour patterns, and exposes prediction results via a Flask API endpoint consumed by the Node.js backend. The ML module to be trained, tested, and integrated by Week 16.
Test and evaluate the full system

Conduct functional testing across all modules, gather feedback from test users, and evaluate how accurately the ML model predicts busy periods against actual order data. Evaluation to be completed by Week 18.
Draw conclusions and recommend best practices

Based on evaluation findings, produce a set of conclusions and practical recommendations regarding the use of weather-responsive interfaces and ML-driven analytics in restaurant technology. Recommendations to be included in the final report.

The project will follow an Agile-inspired development approach, broken into iterative sprints. This suits the nature of the work because requirements may evolve slightly as development progresses and testing reveals gaps. Each sprint will have a defined deliverable, and progress will be reviewed regularly against the objectives set above. The dissertation will be developed alongside the practical work, with sections written as each phase completes rather than leaving everything to the end.
To understand what users actually want from a restaurant app, a short online questionnaire will be distributed to around 20 to 30 participants. The questionnaire will focus on how people currently

use restaurant apps, whether they feel weather influences their food choices, and what information they would find helpful on an admin dashboard. In addition to this, a semi-structured interview will be conducted with a restaurant owner or manager to gather insight into the operational challenges they face, particularly around staffing and demand planning. This primary data will directly inform the system requirements.

The application will follow a three-tier architecture: a frontend layer, a backend API layer, and a database layer. The web frontend will be built in React.js with Tailwind CSS, and the mobile version will use React Native with Expo. The backend will be a RESTful API built in Node.js, handling all business logic and communicating with a MongoDB database. A separate Python microservice, built with Flask, will host the trained Scikit-learn machine learning model for peak hours prediction. Node.js will call this Flask service when the admin requests analytics data.

Two separate interfaces one for customers to manage their accounts, browse the menu, make reservations, and leave feedback; and one for admins to manage the menu, view and confirm reservations, monitor feedback, and access analytics reports.
Customers can select a date, time slot, and number of seats to book a table. Admins can manage available time slots and view upcoming bookings from the dashboard.
Admins can add, edit, and remove menu items including names, descriptions, prices, categories, and images. The menu displayed to customers is always up to date based on what the admin has configured.

The application will connect to the OpenWeatherMap API to retrieve the current weather at the restaurant's location. Based on the temperature and conditions returned, the system will filter and highlight relevant menu items — for example, hot drinks and soups on cold days, salads and cold beverages when it is warm. This logic will be handled on the backend.
A Python script will extract order history data from MongoDB, including timestamps and order volume. Pandas and NumPy will be used for data cleaning and feature engineering

extracting the hour of day, day of week, and whether it is a weekend. A Random Forest model from Scikit-learn will be trained on this data to predict busy periods. The trained model will be served via a Flask API, which the Node.js backend calls to
populate the peak hours report in the admin dashboard. Chart.js will be used on the frontend to visuali
Customers can submit written feedback and star ratings after their visit or order. Admins can view all feedback from the dashboard and use it for service improvement.

One potential challenge is the quality of training data for the machine learning module. Since the system is new, there will be limited real order history initially. To address this, synthetic data will be generated to simulate order patterns for training and testing purposes. Another challenge is the accuracy of weather-based suggestions, which depends on the quality and update frequency of the weather API. The free tier of OpenWeatherMap updates every 10 minutes, which is sufficient for the purposes of this project. Time management across both the development work and the written dissertation will need careful planning.

There are a few ethical considerations that need to be addressed in this project. First, the questionnaire and interview data collected from participants will be handled in line with GDPR principles. Participants will be fully informed about the purpose of the research before taking part, and all responses will be kept anonymous. No personal data will be stored beyond what is necessary for the research, and data will be deleted once the dissertation is submitted.

Regarding the application itself, user accounts and order history stored in MongoDB will be password-protected and access-controlled. Admin and user roles will have clearly separated permissions so that customer data cannot be accessed by unauthori
ed parties. Any test data used during development will be clearly labelled as such and will not include real personal information.

With respect to the machine learning component, the model will be trained on order pattern data rather than any personally identifiable customer information. The predictions it generates will only be used for operational planning purposes within the admin dashboard.

Finally, all academic sources referenced in this dissertation will be properly cited in accordance with the required referencing convention. The work submitted will be entirely the author's own, and AI tools will not be used to produce any written sections of the report.
